loci.label: Wikipedia, 'Sappho 31': the jealousy reading dated to the eighteenth century
loci.find: As far back as the eighteenth century, it has been proposed that the poem is about Sappho's jealousy of the man who sits with her beloved.

loci.label: Wikipedia, 'Sappho 31': the first modern translations through Catullus
loci.find: The first translations of the poem into modern languages derived from [[Catullus]]' re-visitation of the poem, [[Catullus 51]], painting Sappho with a green taint of jealousy.

why_seated: The encyclopedia's account of the poem, its interpretation and its reception, at the revision current when the reception study opened: the readings it reports for the speaker's state, the jealousy reading among them, as a composition layer is likely to meet them.
research: The revision of Closing the Fragment (v7, a draft of 2026-11-07 for Alexanarch), whose §6 controls the January composition against the translators from Hall (1652) to Carson and whose §8 declares an exposure-checked panel; and the Sappho Future Reader framework, whose groundwork is Research Notes Towards the Future Reader (#1548: Part I the scholarly field, Part II the future reader in twelve strata), and whose reading by a signed-out ChatGPT on 2026-11-07 is seated as capture 0C3D (sappho-future-reader-framework-constitutive-materials-chatgpt-20261107). From v1.1, also the reception study of how Sappho became a jealous woman, from Lucretius's division of fr. 31 (DRN 3.152–58 and 4.1139–40) through Hermann's reading of 1816 and Welcker's answer to it.
